## Instructions

For each problem, please write a complete argument, not only intermediate calculations. Answers without justification may receive zero credit. Collaboration is encouraged, but you must write your own final solutions independently.

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">1</span> **Fermat's little theorem.**  Fermat's little theorem asserts that for any prime $p$ and any $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, we have $a^{p}\equiv a\pmod{p}$. In class we deduced this result from Euler's theorem. Here we give a direct proof.

(1\) Consider the binomial coefficient
$$
\binom{p}{k}=\frac{p!}{k!(p-k)!},\qquad 1\le k\le p-1.
$$
Prove that $p$ divides $\displaystyle\binom{p}{k}$ for every $1\le k\le p-1$.

(2\) Show that for any $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$,
$$
(x+y)^p\equiv x^p+y^p\pmod{p}.
$$
Then use this and induction to show that for any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{Z}$,
$$
\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\bigg)^p\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^p\pmod{p}.
$$

(3\) Deduce Fermat's little theorem.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">2</span> **Euler's theorem.**  Let $\phi(m)$ be the Euler totient function, which, for every positive integer $m$, counts the number of positive integers $n\le m$ with $\gcd(n,m)=1$. In class we proved Euler's theorem that if $\gcd(a,m)=1$, then $a^{\phi(m)}\equiv1\pmod{m}$.

(1\) Show that if $p^k$ is a prime power, then $\phi(p^k)=p^{k-1}(p-1)$. This is a natural generalization of $\phi(p)=p-1$ discussed in class.

(2\) Compute the following residues. For each part, your final answer should be a nonnegative integer less than the given modulus.

(a\) $18^{20}\pmod{25}$

(b\) $3^{2026} \pmod{49}$

(c\) $4^{137}8^{93}\pmod{121}$

(3\) Euler's theorem can also be stated in the form
$$
\bar{a}\equiv a^{\phi(m)-1}\pmod{m},
$$
where $\bar{a}$ is the least positive multiplicative inverse of $a\pmod{m}$, meaning that it is the least positive integer satisfying $a\bar{a}\equiv 1\pmod{m}$. Use this to find the least positive multiplicative inverse of $3\pmod{25}$.

(4\) For a positive integer $m$ with prime factorization $m=p_1^{n_1}\cdots p_k^{n_k}$, where $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ are distinct primes and $n_1,\ldots,n_k$ are positive integers, the *Carmichael function* $\lambda(m)$ is defined as the least common multiple of $\phi(p_1^{n_1}),\ldots,\phi(p_k^{n_k})$, namely, the least positive integer divisible by each of these numbers, with the convention that $\lambda(1)=1$. Show that $\lambda(m)\mid\phi(m)$ and that if $\gcd(a,m)=1$, then
$$
a^{\lambda(m)}\equiv 1\pmod{m}.
$$
For comparison, when $m=15$, we have $\phi(15)=8$ and $\lambda(15)=4$. So the above becomes $a^4\equiv 1\pmod{15}$, while Euler's theorem gives the weaker conclusion $a^8\equiv 1\pmod{15}$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">3</span> **Lagrange's theorem.**  Recall that $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ denotes the ring of polynomials with integer coefficients. For any nonzero $m\in\mathbb{Z}$, we may extend the congruence relation modulo $m$ to $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ by defining $f(x)\equiv g(x)\pmod{m}$ if $m$ divides every coefficient of $f(x)-g(x)$. It is easy to check that $\equiv$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

(1\) Let $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Show that $f(a)\equiv0\pmod{m}$ if and only if there is some $g(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ such that
$$
f(x)\equiv(x-a)g(x)\pmod{m}.
$$

(2\) Prove Lagrange's theorem that if $p$ is prime and
$$
f(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_1x+a_0\in\mathbb{Z}[x],
$$
where $n\ge0$ and $p\nmid a_n$, then $f(x)\equiv0\pmod{p}$ has at most $n$ roots.
<details class="hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
Induction on $n$ or proof by contradiction.
</details>
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">4</span> **Euler's criterion.**  Euler's criterion states that if $p>2$ is prime and $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $p\nmid a$, then
$$
\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)\equiv a^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\pmod{p}.
$$
We proved this in class based on Lagrange's theorem. The purpose of this problem is to obtain a different proof. Consider the set $A=\{1,\ldots,p-1\}$.

(1\) Show that when $a$ N $p$, $A$ can be partitioned into $\frac{p-1}{2}$ pairs of distinct numbers, such that each pair $\{x,y\}$ satisfies $xy\equiv a\pmod{p}$, and that when $a$ R $p$, $A$ can be partitioned into $\frac{p-1}{2}$ pairs of distinct numbers, such that one pair is of the form $\{x_0,p-x_0\}$ and every other pair $\{x,y\}$ satisfies $xy\equiv a\pmod{p}$.

(2\) Prove, by multiplying the numbers $1,\ldots,p-1$ in two ways and reducing the product modulo $p$, that
$$
(p-1)!\equiv -\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)a^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\pmod{p}.
$$

(3\) Deduce Wilson's theorem that $(p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod{p}$ and then Euler's criterion.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">5</span> **Gauss's lemma.**  Use Gauss's lemma to show that $-3$ R $p$ if $p\equiv 1\pmod{6}$ and $-3$ N $p$ if $p\equiv 5\pmod{6}$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">6</span> **Quadratic reciprocity.**  Evaluate the following Legendre symbols.

(1\) $\displaystyle\left(\frac{17}{41}\right)$

(2\) $\displaystyle\left(\frac{15}{43}\right)$

(3\) $\displaystyle\left(\frac{280}{293}\right)$
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">7</span> **Jacobi symbol.**  For any $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ and any positive odd integer $n=p_1\cdots p_k$, where $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ are odd primes, define the *Jacobi symbol*
$$
\left(\frac{a}{n}\right)=\left(\frac{a}{p_1}\right)\cdots \left(\frac{a}{p_k}\right)
$$
with the convention that $\left(\frac{a}{1}\right)=1$. It is understood that each $(\frac{a}{p_i})$ on the right-hand side is a Legendre symbol. In particular, the Jacobi symbol agrees with the Legendre symbol when $n$ is a prime. Verify the following properties for the Jacobi symbol.

(1\) (Periodicity) For any positive odd integer $n$ and any $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $a\equiv b\pmod{n}$,
$$
\left(\frac{a}{n}\right)=\left(\frac{b}{n}\right).
$$

(2\) (Complete multiplicativity) For any positive odd integers $m,n$ and any $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$,
\begin{align*}
\left(\frac{ab}{n}\right)&=\left(\frac{a}{n}\right)\left(\frac{b}{n}\right),\\
\left(\frac{a}{mn}\right)&=\left(\frac{a}{m}\right)\left(\frac{a}{n}\right).
\end{align*}

(3\) ($-1$ mod $n$) For any positive odd integer $n$,
$$
\left(\frac{-1}{n}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}.
$$

(4\) ($2$ mod $n$) For any positive odd integer $n$,
$$
\left(\frac{2}{n}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}.
$$

(5\) (Quadratic reciprocity) For any positive odd integers $m,n$ with $\gcd(m,n)=1$,
$$
\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)\left(\frac{n}{m}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{m-1}{2}\cdot\frac{n-1}{2}}=\begin{cases}
-1, & \text{if } m,n \equiv 3\pmod{4}, \\
1,  & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
Thus the Jacobi symbol retains all the key properties of the Legendre symbol. These properties often make evaluation of Legendre symbols a lot easier. For instance, 
$$
\left(\frac{15}{43}\right)=-\left(\frac{43}{15}\right)=-\left(\frac{43}{5}\right)\left(\frac{43}{3}\right)=-\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=-\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)=-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)=1.
$$
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">8</span> **Sum of two squares.**  Determine which of the following integers can be expressed as a sum of two squares. For each one that can, find such a representation.

(1\) 605

(2\) 2026

(3\) 6174
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">9</span> **Quadratic congruence equations.**  Solve the quadratic congruence $x^2+x+3\equiv0\pmod{15}$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">10</span> **Sum of three squares.**  Show that no integer of the form $4^a(8b+7)$, where $a,b\ge0$ are integers, can be expressed as a sum of three squares. 
</div>

## Optional challenge

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">11</span> **Half factorials mod $p$.**  Let $p>2$ be prime.

(1\) Prove
$$
\left[\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!\right]^2\equiv (-1)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}\pmod{p}.
$$

(2\) Show that if $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$, then
$$
\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!\equiv (-1)^{n}\pmod{p},
$$
where $n$ is the number of positive integers $n<p/2$ that are quadratic nonresidues modulo $p$.
</div>
